name: Numerical Label Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun (basic or complex) following an embellishment noun; bare NP
dimensions.meaning: Rigid designation of a unique entity via numerical identifier
dimensions.function: Names/identifies specific entities (rooms, highways, addresses, etc.)
dimensions.distribution: Subject, object, complement positions; typically without determiner

1.definition: A cardinal proper noun heads a bare NP used as a proper name, identifying a unique entity through direct reference

examples.note: Numerical label identifying a specific room
Numerical label for a specific highway

constraints.description: Cardinal noun heads a bare NP; resists determiners and attributive modifiers.
Rigidly designates a unique entity; reference is direct, not mediated by descriptive content.
The non-numeral element (Room, Highway, etc.) functions as embellishment, not attributive modifier.

relatedConstructions.notes: This subtype restricts the identifier to numerical forms. The wider pattern also admits letters and mixed codes.
Reynolds treats 1066 in the year 1066 as an appositive (n. 10). A bare year such as 1066 can identify a calendar year on its own.

grounds.locator: §5, cardinal nouns used as labels (§5.2 [7a–b] and nn. 9–10); §2, terminology

grounds.note: CGEL lists Ward 17 among composite heads and calls Ward a descriptor inside the name. Its embellishments are semantically non-restrictive dependents outside the name, and they include nominal and adjectival attributive modifiers. So CGEL doesn't contrast embellishment with attributive modifier, as the third constraint (from Reynolds 2026, n. 9) does.

grounds.locator: Meeting Locations, Robert Purcell Community Center
grounds.note: Lists Room 101 as the code for the TV Lounge.

projection.target: In room six, six identifies a designated room in the labeling system. It does not say that six rooms are involved. Adding an external quantity in two Room Six signs can count the signs while leaving the label unchanged.
projection.evidence: Reynolds includes label uses among cardinal proper-noun uses and distinguishes the label from count determination.

known_boundary_items: In 20 Pheasant Street the number precedes the street name, unlike Room 101 and Flight 447.
Room 302A has the same naming function with a mixed code, as covered by the wider descriptor-plus-identifier entry.

curious.title: Names made of numbers
curious.summary: A word like Room or Highway followed by a number can work as the name of one particular thing.
curious.body: Some places and things are named with a number. Room 101 is one specific room, Highway 401 is one specific highway, and Flight 447 is one specific flight. In these names the number doesn't count anything. It says which room, which highway or which flight you mean. That's why the number behaves like part of a name rather than like a quantity. Compare Room 101 with 101 rooms: in the second, the number tells you how many rooms there are. In the first, it picks out a single room in a system of labels.
curious.try: Try swapping the number in a name you know, such as a room or a flight. Do you now mean a different thing, or a different amount of the same thing?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining why a number after a noun like Room can be a name rather than a quantity.
teacher.explain: In Room 101, the number is a cardinal noun that names the thing, and the whole phrase is a bare NP (it has no determiner of its own) used as a proper name. On this dictionary's analysis, the first word, Room, is an embellishment of the name rather than an attributive modifier, and it gives the kind of thing named. The number doesn't say how many: it points to one unique entity through a labelling system. Compare 101 rooms, where 101 is a quantity that counts rooms. In 20 Pheasant Street the number comes first, before the street name, unlike Room 101 and Flight 447.
teacher.terms: Cardinal noun: a number word used as a noun. Embellishment: this dictionary's label for the non-numeral word (Room, Highway). CGEL analyzes the comparable Ward in Ward 17 differently, as a descriptor inside the name.
watch_for: A learner might read Room 101 as one hundred and one rooms.
A learner might think 20 Pheasant Street is a count of something rather than an address.
teacher.activity: Give pairs of cards, one showing a label (Highway 401, Flight 447) and one showing a quantity (401 highways, 447 flights). Students sort them into "names one thing" and "counts things", then say how they decided.

child.hook: If you're in Room 101, are you in a hundred and one rooms?
child.explain: Sometimes a number is a name. Room 101 is just one room, and the number tells you which one. In 101 rooms, the number tells you how many.
child.play: Find numbers on doors, buses or signs. For each one, decide if it names one thing or counts several.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms no longer glosses embellishment as CGEL's term for Room (CGEL treats the comparable Ward as a descriptor inside the name); teacher.explain marks the embellishment analysis as this dictionary's.
